Identifiability and partial identification under spatial confounding in additive risk models

SHENG PAN
Abstract

In spatial risk attribution, continuous environmental exposures and unmeasured background factors often co-vary across broad geographic scales, making it difficult to separate true exposure effects from spatial confounding using finite disease counts. Existing remedies typically project out or penalize shared spatial trends, leaving unclear whether estimation instability stems from the overall capacity of the latent random field or from its directional alignment with exposure. By decomposing the Fisher-weighted smoothing operator of an additive Poisson point process model, we show that while effective degrees of freedom measure total smoothing capacity, the relative loss of Fisher information for the exposure coefficient is governed solely by a distinct directional quantity that we call penalized collinear overlap. Rotating the spatial kernel alters this information loss while holding total capacity fixed, implying that no single smoothing scale is universally optimal. Because real-world confounding combines smooth regional trends with sharp local jumps that escape any moderate basis dictionary, point identification remains fragile. We therefore develop a partial identification framework that bounds residual confounding bias using an observable benchmark covariate. Projecting a joint spatial confidence ellipse yields valid intervals even under weak benchmarks, while incorporating a negative control outcome sharpens the bounds and flags assumption violations. Simulation studies and an analysis of childhood respiratory mortality across England demonstrate the method.

Key words. Partial identification, Penalized smoothing, Sensitivity analysis, Spatial confounding, Spatial point process.

1 Introduction

In spatial epidemiology and environmental risk assessment, researchers often combine continuous environmental exposure surfaces, uneven population denominators recorded by administrative units, and unmeasured background risk within a single model. To avoid ecological bias from coarsening continuous variables over administrative boundaries, embedding all three components into an inhomogeneous Poisson point process over continuous space has become a standard strategy (Best et al., 2000; Gotway & Young, 2002). Although continuous-space modeling resolves external aggregation bias, it moves the identifiability problem inside the model. Environmental exposures and unmeasured neighborhood risks such as socioeconomic deprivation or housing quality tend to cluster over the same geographic areas. Consequently, the spatial latent random field introduced to absorb background risk inevitably overlaps with exposure over smooth spatial scales. Whenever the smoothing scale or roughness penalty chosen for the working model does not match the spatial correlation structure of the true unmeasured confounding field, finite disease counts cannot separate the main exposure effect from the background field, causing substantial drift in the estimated exposure slope.

Recent methodological work has proposed several adjustment strategies to address spatial confounding and regression identifiability (Paciorek, 2010; Khan & Calder, 2022; Dupont et al., 2022; Guillaumin et al., 2022; Guan et al., 2023; Bolin & Wallin, 2026; Datta & Stein, 2026; Khan & Berrett, 2026; Wiecha et al., 2025). Existing approaches follow three main mechanisms. The first group uses orthogonal projection, such as restricted spatial regression (Khan & Calder, 2022), which forces the spatial latent field to be orthogonal to the exposure vector so that variance inflation from shared directions disappears. The second group uses two-stage residualization, such as the spatial plus method (Dupont et al., 2022), which removes smooth spatial trends from exposure via a spatial smoother and enters the high-frequency exposure residuals into the health outcome model alongside a spatial random effect. The third group uses spectral filtering (Guillaumin et al., 2022; Guan et al., 2023), which transforms observations on regular grids or graphs into the frequency domain and dampens shared low-frequency components. Each approach enjoys appealing properties when its structural assumptions hold.

Yet methods aimed at restoring a single point estimate rely on strong identifying assumptions. Orthogonal projection assumes that any variation along spatial directions shared by exposure and background risk belongs entirely to the exposure effect. Two-stage residualization assumes that exposure and unmeasured confounding share the exact same smooth basis space. Spectral filtering assumes that unmeasured confounding lives strictly in low-frequency bands on a regular domain. In practice, real unmeasured confounding combines smooth regional trends of unknown scale with sharp local jumps across neighborhood boundaries, housing estates, and socioeconomic clusters. When this mixed spatial variation extends outside the span of the chosen basis dictionary, no single-scale smoother or forced orthogonal projection can prevent omitted confounding bias and collinear variance inflation simultaneously. Bounding and identifying exposure effects when unmeasured confounding has an unknown spatial structure thus remains a central methodological problem.

To address this challenge, we move away from fragile point identification under a single smoothing model and develop a partial identification framework for the Poisson point process additive risk model. Our work makes three main contributions.

First, using a reproducing kernel operator framework weighted by local Poisson Fisher information, we show that the loss of effective information for the exposure coefficient is governed by a directional alignment measure that we call penalized collinear overlap, rather than by the effective degrees of freedom of the basis space. Building on this spectral decomposition, we show that no single spatial basis dominates all others, meaning that no single smoothing scale can maximize effective information across all exposure patterns.

Second, because unmeasured confounding in applications includes sharp local variation outside any moderate basis dictionary, we develop a design-stage orthogonalization and partial identification method. We combine known covariates and multi-scale spatial kernels into a baseline dictionary, and introduce an observable benchmark variable that shares a similar spatial clustering mechanism with unmeasured background risk. The change in the orthogonalized exposure estimate before and after adding this benchmark variable measures how much bias a representative background factor removes, which we use to bound the remaining unmeasured confounding bias. To form valid confidence intervals even when the benchmark shift is close to zero, we construct a spatial heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix using residuals cleaned by a dense auxiliary basis, and project a two-dimensional joint confidence ellipse onto the target parameter axis.

Third, relying on a benchmark variable alone leaves two practical gaps. The benchmark shift does not reveal the sign of the remaining bias, which forces symmetric intervals around the adjusted estimate, and a researcher-chosen sensitivity multiplier cannot be falsified by covariate data alone. To close these gaps, we incorporate a negative control outcome recorded on the same spatial units that is unaffected by exposure but shares the same neighborhood background confounding. Any association between exposure and the negative control outcome after baseline adjustment directly reflects remaining background bias. Combining the benchmark variable with the negative control outcome in a three-dimensional confidence ellipsoid narrows the interval and flags cases where the two sources of evidence conflict. We also provide three diagnostic checks to verify before reporting whether the data support the maintained assumptions.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 sets up the continuous-space Poisson point process additive risk model. Section 3 derives the spectral decomposition of latent field flexibility, the benchmark partial identification interval, the joint ellipse projection confidence interval, the negative control calibration, and the pre-reporting diagnostic checks. Section 4 reports three Monte Carlo simulation experiments, and Section 5 applies the workflow to childhood respiratory mortality across England. Section 6 concludes.

Conversely, if λ\lambda is made very small so the latent field becomes highly flexible, the kernel basis absorbs spatial variation belonging to exposure itself, draining effective Fisher information for β\beta and inflating its variance. We next examine the geometry of this trade-off.

3 Diagnostics of Latent Field Flexibility and Partial Identification

The effective degrees of freedom EDF⁡(λ)\mathrm{EDF}(\lambda) sums the shrinkage factors σj2/(σj2+λ)\sigma_{j}^{2}/(\sigma_{j}^{2}+\lambda) with equal weight across all basis directions, measuring total fitting capacity regardless of where the exposure vector points. Proposition 1 shows that this directional overlap, rather than total capacity, governs the effective information left for estimating β\beta.

When η=1\eta=1, meaning that 𝒙~\tilde{\bm{x}} lies entirely inside the column space of 𝑩\bm{B}, the unpenalized effective information vanishes and local identifiability fails in the unpenalized limit.

The proof is given in the Supplementary Material, Section .

Proposition 1 makes clear that changing the kernel scale ℓ\ell rotates the singular directions 𝒖B,j\bm{u}_{B,j} relative to 𝒙W\bm{x}_{W}. Consequently, two spatial bases can have the exact same effective degrees of freedom EDF⁡(λ)\mathrm{EDF}(\lambda), yet whichever basis aligns more closely with the dominant spatial pattern of exposure suffers a much larger drop in effective information. As formalized in Lemma  of the Supplementary Material (Section ), whenever two candidate kernel bases have non-nested column spaces, neither basis yields uniformly larger unpenalized effective information across all exposure patterns.

To see how ηpen​(λ)\eta_{\mathrm{pen}}(\lambda) shapes bias and variance simultaneously, consider the whitened linear working model for the residualized working response 𝒚W=𝒙W​β+𝒇W+𝜺W\bm{y}_{W}=\bm{x}_{W}\beta+\bm{f}_{W}+\bm{\varepsilon}_{W} at fixed weights 𝑾\bm{W}, where 𝒇W=𝑾1/2​(𝑰n−𝑷H)​𝒇\bm{f}_{W}=\bm{W}^{1/2}(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{H})\bm{f} is the whitened true confounding field, 𝜺W\bm{\varepsilon}_{W} is the zero-mean whitened working noise with conditional covariance 𝑰n−𝑾1/2𝑷H𝑾−1/2\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{W}^{1/2}\bm{P}_{H}\bm{W}^{-1/2}, and 𝒙W,⟂=(𝑰n−𝑼B​𝑼B𝖳)​𝒙W\bm{x}_{W,\perp}=(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{U}_{B}\bm{U}_{B}^{\mathsf{T}})\bm{x}_{W} is the component of exposure orthogonal to the basis space. 3.2 Benchmark Partial Identification under Residual Confounding

Because the spatial scale of unmeasured confounding is unknown in practice, tuning a single smoothing parameter cannot eliminate omitted confounding bias without risking severe variance inflation. A natural first step is to combine the known covariates 𝑯\bm{H} with spatial kernel bases 𝑭\bm{F} spanning several bandwidths into a baseline dictionary 𝒁=[𝑯,𝑭]\bm{Z}=[\bm{H},\bm{F}], removing all linear and smooth trends within the span of 𝒁\bm{Z} at the design stage. Even so, the number of basis functions in 𝒁\bm{Z} must remain moderate so that 𝒁\bm{Z} does not absorb all variation in 𝒙\bm{x}. Sharp local jumps in background risk across neighborhood boundaries therefore remain outside the column space of 𝒁\bm{Z}, leaving residual confounding that invalidates point identification.

In the additive risk model (1), the observed counts satisfy 𝔼[𝒀∣𝒟,𝒇]=𝑾o𝒎\mathbb{E}[\bm{Y}\mid\mathcal{D},\bm{f}]=\bm{W}_{o}\bm{m} with 𝒎=𝑯​𝜷H+β​𝒙+𝒇\bm{m}=\bm{H}\bm{\beta}_{H}+\beta\bm{x}+\bm{f}. To estimate β\beta while removing 𝑯​𝜷H\bm{H}\bm{\beta}_{H} and all confounding components inside the column space of 𝒁\bm{Z}, we regress the empirical incidence rates 𝑾o−1​𝒀\bm{W}_{o}^{-1}\bm{Y} on [𝒙,𝒁][\bm{x},\bm{Z}] using the known design-stage offset weights 𝑾o\bm{W}_{o}. Because 𝑾o\bm{W}_{o} does not depend on 𝒀\bm{Y}, the resulting estimator is linear in the counts. Let 𝑷Z=𝒁​(𝒁𝖳​𝑾o​𝒁)+​𝒁𝖳​𝑾o\bm{P}_{Z}=\bm{Z}(\bm{Z}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o}\bm{Z})^{+}\bm{Z}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o} denote the 𝑾o\bm{W}_{o}-weighted projection onto the column space of 𝒁\bm{Z}, 𝒓=(𝑰n−𝑷Z)​𝒙\bm{r}=(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{Z})\bm{x} the residualized exposure vector, and Jn=𝒓𝖳​𝑾o​𝒓J_{n}=\bm{r}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o}\bm{r} the remaining exposure information. By the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, the baseline orthogonalized estimator is β^=𝒒𝖳​𝑾o−1​𝒀=𝒄𝖳​𝒀\hat{\beta}=\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o}^{-1}\bm{Y}=\bm{c}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{Y} with weight vectors

𝒒=𝑾o​𝒓Jn,𝒄=𝑾o−1​𝒒=𝒓Jn,\bm{q}=\frac{\bm{W}_{o}\bm{r}}{J_{n}},\qquad\bm{c}=\bm{W}_{o}^{-1}\bm{q}=\frac{\bm{r}}{J_{n}}, (10)

which satisfy 𝒒𝖳​𝒙=1\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{x}=1 and 𝒒𝖳​𝒁=𝟎𝖳\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{Z}=\bm{0}^{\mathsf{T}}.

The orthogonality property 𝒒𝖳​𝒁=𝟎𝖳\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{Z}=\bm{0}^{\mathsf{T}} eliminates both 𝑯​𝜷H\bm{H}\bm{\beta}_{H} and the smooth confounding projection 𝑷Z​𝒇\bm{P}_{Z}\bm{f}. However, when the residual confounding component 𝒇⟂=(𝑰n−𝑷Z)​𝒇\bm{f}_{\perp}=(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{Z})\bm{f} outside the span of 𝒁\bm{Z} is nonzero, the conditional mean θ0=𝔼[β^∣𝒟,𝒇]=𝒒𝖳𝒎=β+𝒒𝖳𝒇\theta_{0}=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}\mid\mathcal{D},\bm{f}]=\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{m}=\beta+\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{f} differs from β\beta by a bias b0=θ0−β=𝒒𝖳​𝒇⟂b_{0}=\theta_{0}-\beta=\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{f}_{\perp} that does not vanish as sample size grows. Because 𝒇⟂\bm{f}_{\perp} is unobserved, the baseline dictionary alone cannot bound b0b_{0}.

Following sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding in causal inference (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020; Ciocănea-Teodorescu et al., 2022; Tan, 2024; Dorn et al., 2025), we introduce an observable benchmark variable 𝑽∈ℝn×pv\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p_{v}} capturing a representative mechanism of local confounding outside 𝒁\bm{Z}. As shown in Figure 1, 𝑽\bm{V} is chosen from domain knowledge as a measured neighborhood factor, such as socioeconomic deprivation, that co-occurs with both high exposure 𝒙\bm{x} and elevated baseline disease risk 𝒀\bm{Y} and retains variation outside 𝒁\bm{Z} so that (𝑰n−𝑷Z)​𝑽≠𝟎(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{Z})\bm{V}\neq\bm{0}.

Adding 𝑽\bm{V} to the baseline dictionary forms the augmented dictionary 𝒁aug=[𝒁,𝑽]\bm{Z}_{\mathrm{aug}}=[\bm{Z},\bm{V}]. Let 𝑷Zaug=𝒁aug​(𝒁aug𝖳​𝑾o​𝒁aug)+​𝒁aug𝖳​𝑾o\bm{P}_{Z_{\mathrm{aug}}}=\bm{Z}_{\mathrm{aug}}(\bm{Z}_{\mathrm{aug}}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o}\bm{Z}_{\mathrm{aug}})^{+}\bm{Z}_{\mathrm{aug}}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o} be the corresponding projection matrix, 𝒓a=(𝑰n−𝑷Zaug)​𝒙\bm{r}_{a}=(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{Z_{\mathrm{aug}}})\bm{x} the augmented exposure residual, and Ja,n=𝒓a𝖳​𝑾o​𝒓a>0J_{a,n}=\bm{r}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o}\bm{r}_{a}>0 the remaining exposure information. The augmented weight vector 𝒒a\bm{q}_{a} and estimator β^aug\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}} are

𝒒a=𝑾o​(𝑰n−𝑷Zaug)​𝒙‖(𝑰n−𝑷Zaug)​𝒙‖𝑾o2=𝑾o​𝒓aJa,n,β^aug=𝒄a𝖳​𝒀=∑j=1nqa,joj​Yj,\bm{q}_{a}=\frac{\bm{W}_{o}(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{Z_{\mathrm{aug}}})\bm{x}}{\|(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{Z_{\mathrm{aug}}})\bm{x}\|_{\bm{W}_{o}}^{2}}=\frac{\bm{W}_{o}\bm{r}_{a}}{J_{a,n}},\qquad\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}}=\bm{c}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{Y}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{q_{a,j}}{o_{j}}Y_{j}, (11)

where 𝒄a=𝑾o−1​𝒒a=𝒓a/Ja,n\bm{c}_{a}=\bm{W}_{o}^{-1}\bm{q}_{a}=\bm{r}_{a}/J_{a,n}, satisfying 𝒒a𝖳​𝒙=1\bm{q}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{x}=1 and 𝒒a𝖳​𝒁aug=𝟎𝖳\bm{q}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{Z}_{\mathrm{aug}}=\bm{0}^{\mathsf{T}}. Its conditional expectation θa=𝔼[β^aug∣𝒟,𝒇]=𝒒a𝖳𝒎\theta_{a}=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}}\mid\mathcal{D},\bm{f}]=\bm{q}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{m} has remaining bias ba=θa−β=𝒒a𝖳​𝒇b_{a}=\theta_{a}-\beta=\bm{q}_{a}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{f}. The difference between the baseline and augmented estimates defines the sample benchmark shift,

d^=β^−β^aug,\hat{d}=\hat{\beta}-\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}},

whose population expectation is d0=𝔼[d^∣𝒟,𝒇]=(𝒒−𝒒a)𝖳𝒎=b0−bad_{0}=\mathbb{E}[\hat{d}\mid\mathcal{D},\bm{f}]=(\bm{q}-\bm{q}_{a})^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{m}=b_{0}-b_{a}. The magnitude |d0||d_{0}| measures the exact amount of confounding bias removed by adjusting for 𝑽\bm{V}. If the remaining unmeasured bias |ba||b_{a}| after adjusting for 𝑽\bm{V} is at most Γ\Gamma times the bias shift |d0||d_{0}| produced by 𝑽\bm{V}, we obtain a partial identification interval for β\beta.

Assumption 1.

For a given relative confounding multiplier Γ≥0\Gamma\geq 0, the remaining population bias satisfies |ba|≤Γ​|d0||b_{a}|\leq\Gamma|d_{0}|.

Theorem 1.

Under Assumption 1, the true exposure effect β\beta lies in the closed interval

β∈ΘΓ=[θa−Γ​|d0|,θa+Γ​|d0|].\beta\in\Theta_{\Gamma}=\big[\theta_{a}-\Gamma|d_{0}|,\ \theta_{a}+\Gamma|d_{0}|\big]. (12)

3.3 Joint Spatial Covariance and Ellipse Projection Intervals

To turn the population interval ΘΓ=[θa−Γ​|d0|,θa+Γ​|d0|]\Theta_{\Gamma}=[\theta_{a}-\Gamma|d_{0}|,\ \theta_{a}+\Gamma|d_{0}|] into a sample confidence interval with level 1−α1-\alpha, we use the two-dimensional statistic 𝑻^=(β^aug,d^)𝖳\hat{\bm{T}}=(\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}},\hat{d})^{\mathsf{T}} estimating 𝑻=(θa,d0)𝖳\bm{T}=(\theta_{a},d_{0})^{\mathsf{T}}. Directly plugging β^aug\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}} and |d^||\hat{d}| into the endpoints and applying the delta method fails when the benchmark variable has a weak effect so that d0d_{0} is close to zero, because the absolute value function has a sharp corner at zero and |d^||\hat{d}| follows a folded normal distribution rather than a Gaussian law.

To avoid this corner problem without splitting cases, we build a smooth joint confidence ellipse for 𝑻=(θa,d0)𝖳\bm{T}=(\theta_{a},d_{0})^{\mathsf{T}} and project that ellipse onto the one-dimensional interval endpoints. Because both β^aug\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}} and d^\hat{d} are linear in 𝒀\bm{Y}, their sampling error is a linear sum of the centered count errors ϵj=Yj−μj\epsilon_{j}=Y_{j}-\mu_{j}, written in vector form as ϵ=𝒀−𝝁\bm{\epsilon}=\bm{Y}-\bm{\mu},

3.4 Negative Control Calibration and Diagnostic Checks

Although Theorem 2 yields a valid confidence interval from the benchmark variable 𝑽\bm{V} alone, two practical limitations remain. First, because the sign of the remaining bias bab_{a} is unknown, the interval must expand symmetrically by ±Γ​|d0|\pm\Gamma|d_{0}| on both sides of θa\theta_{a}. Second, for any multiplier Γ≥0\Gamma\geq 0, (14) always returns a nonempty interval, so covariate information alone cannot warn the analyst if the assumed bound |ba|≤Γ​|d0||b_{a}|\leq\Gamma|d_{0}| is contradicted by reality.

To overcome both limitations, we introduce a negative control outcome vector 𝒀NC\bm{Y}_{\mathrm{NC}} with entries (YNC,1,…,YNC,n)𝖳(Y_{\mathrm{NC},1},\dots,Y_{\mathrm{NC},n})^{\mathsf{T}} observed across the same nn spatial units. A valid negative control outcome is a health count that is not causally affected by exposure 𝒙\bm{x}, but is driven by the same unmeasured neighborhood confounding 𝒇\bm{f} as the primary disease outcome. Because 𝒙\bm{x} has no true effect on 𝒀NC\bm{Y}_{\mathrm{NC}}, any residual association between 𝒙\bm{x} and 𝒀NC\bm{Y}_{\mathrm{NC}} after removing the baseline dictionary 𝒁\bm{Z} directly reflects the direction and size of the uneliminated spatial bias. This outcome-side signal trims away parts of the symmetric benchmark interval with the wrong bias sign, and alerts the researcher whenever the bias implied by the negative control conflicts with the benchmark bound.

Parallel to (1), for a negative control outcome 𝒀NC\bm{Y}_{\mathrm{NC}} with known positive baseline offsets 𝒐NC=(oNC,1,…,oNC,n)𝖳\bm{o}_{\mathrm{NC}}=(o_{\mathrm{NC},1},\dots,o_{\mathrm{NC},n})^{\mathsf{T}} and 𝑾o,NC=diag⁡(𝒐NC)\bm{W}_{o,\mathrm{NC}}=\operatorname{diag}(\bm{o}_{\mathrm{NC}}), we have

𝔼[𝒀NC∣𝒟,𝒇]=𝑾o,NC𝒎NC,𝒎NC=𝑯𝜷H,NC+ρNC𝒇+𝝃NC>𝟎,\mathbb{E}[\bm{Y}_{\mathrm{NC}}\mid\mathcal{D},\bm{f}]=\bm{W}_{o,\mathrm{NC}}\bm{m}_{\mathrm{NC}},\qquad\bm{m}_{\mathrm{NC}}=\bm{H}\bm{\beta}_{H,\mathrm{NC}}+\rho_{\mathrm{NC}}\bm{f}+\bm{\xi}_{\mathrm{NC}}>\bm{0}, (15)

where 𝒙\bm{x} does not enter 𝒎NC\bm{m}_{\mathrm{NC}}, ρNC∈ℝ\rho_{\mathrm{NC}}\in\mathbb{R} scales how strongly 𝒇\bm{f} affects the control outcome relative to the primary outcome, and 𝝃NC∈ℝn\bm{\xi}_{\mathrm{NC}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is outcome-specific background variation. Applying the baseline orthogonal weights 𝒒\bm{q} from (10) to the empirical rates of the control outcome defines

τ^NC=∑j=1nqjYNC,joNC,j=𝒒𝖳𝑾o,NC−1𝒀NC,τNC=𝔼[τ^NC∣𝒟,𝒇]=𝒒𝖳𝒎NC.\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{NC}}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}q_{j}\frac{Y_{\mathrm{NC},j}}{o_{\mathrm{NC},j}}=\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{W}_{o,\mathrm{NC}}^{-1}\bm{Y}_{\mathrm{NC}},\qquad\tau_{\mathrm{NC}}=\mathbb{E}[\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{NC}}\mid\mathcal{D},\bm{f}]=\bm{q}^{\mathsf{T}}\bm{m}_{\mathrm{NC}}.

4 Monte Carlo Simulation Study

We conduct three Monte Carlo experiments to evaluate finite-sample performance across point identification, partial identification, and negative control calibration. The first experiment evaluates representative point-identification estimators for spatial confounding when the true confounding scale departs from the working basis, namely two-stage spatial residualization (‘Spatial+‘; Dupont et al. 2022), precision-weighted restricted spatial regression (‘W-RSR‘; Khan & Calder 2022), and spectral high-pass filtering at cutoff scales h=400​mh=400\,\mathrm{m} and h=1500​mh=1500\,\mathrm{m} (‘Spectral‘ h=400​mh=400\,\mathrm{m} and h=1500​mh=1500\,\mathrm{m}; Guan et al. 2023), which operationalize frequency-domain deconfounding in the spirit of the debiased spatial Whittle likelihood (Guillaumin et al., 2022), alongside unadjusted regression, single-scale Gaussian process smoothing, and the Γ=0\Gamma=0 multi-scale orthogonal limit of our framework. Because Experiment 1 shows that all point-identification estimators suffer severe under-coverage under out-of-span local confounding, the second experiment holds the population partial-identification set ΘΓ\Theta_{\Gamma} fixed and compares our joint ellipse projection interval from Theorem 2 against established partial-identification and sensitivity-analysis intervals, including the fixed-length endpoint interval of Imbens & Manski (2004), the length-pretest interval of Stoye (2009), an unadjusted benchmark sensitivity rule without multi-scale spatial orthogonalization (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020; Ciocănea-Teodorescu et al., 2022; Tan, 2024; Dorn et al., 2025), covariance ablations (oracle, unweighted, diagonal, and Bonferroni), and the empirical breakdown point Γ^∗\hat{\Gamma}^{\ast} (Masten & Poirier, 2020). The third experiment assesses how the negative control calibration in Proposition 3 sharpens inference when the bridging condition holds and detects misspecification through empty confidence sets when it is violated.

4.1 Data-Generating Mechanism and Evaluation Metrics

The spatial domain is a square D=(0,6250]2mD=(0,6250]^{2}\,\mathrm{m} partitioned into a 25×2525\times 25 regular grid of spacing 250​m250\,\mathrm{m} with n=625n=625 cells and centroids 𝒔j\bm{s}_{j}. Baseline offsets are drawn independently from log⁡oj∼𝒩⁡(0,0.452)\log o_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.45^{2}) and rescaled to sample mean 11. All continuous spatial components below are centered to sample mean 00 and scaled to unit sample variance.

To generate spatial confounding that combines smooth regional trends with sharp local jumps, we construct three latent spatial fields on the grid. The first is a smooth Gaussian field 𝒇S\bm{f}_{\mathrm{S}} with a Matérn correlation function of smoothness order 3/23/2 and range ℓtrue\ell_{\mathrm{true}}. The second is the observed benchmark variable 𝑽\bm{V}, formed as the standardized equal-weight sum of a short-range Matérn field with range 150​m150\,\mathrm{m} and a block-constant field over a 5×55\times 5 partition of DD into 2525 squares of side 1250​m1250\,\mathrm{m} with independent standard normal block values. The third is an unobserved block-jump field 𝒖\bm{u} defined on the same 5×55\times 5 partition, whose block values have correlation ρblock∈[0,1]\rho_{\mathrm{block}}\in[0,1] with the block component of 𝑽\bm{V}. When ρblock=0\rho_{\mathrm{block}}=0, the benchmark 𝑽\bm{V} carries no information about the unobserved jumps 𝒖\bm{u}.

The true confounding field 𝒇\bm{f} and the exposure vector 𝒙\bm{x} are both generated from these three components. Specifically, the confounding field is

𝒇=a1​𝒇S+a2​𝑽+a3​𝒖,\bm{f}=a_{1}\bm{f}_{\mathrm{S}}+a_{2}\bm{V}+a_{3}\bm{u}, (20)

and the exposure is generated proportionally to 0.5​𝒇S+0.5​𝑽+0.4​𝒖+𝜼0.5\bm{f}_{\mathrm{S}}+0.5\bm{V}+0.4\bm{u}+\bm{\eta} with independent normal noise ηj∼𝒩⁡(0,0.72)\eta_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.7^{2}) and standardized to unit variance. Disease counts are drawn from Yj∼Poisson⁡(oj​mj)Y_{j}\sim\mathrm{Poisson}(o_{j}m_{j}) with additive rate mj=βH,0+β​xj+fjm_{j}=\beta_{H,0}+\beta x_{j}+f_{j} at true parameter β=0.32\beta=0.32, where βH,0=max⁡{2.0, 0.5−mink⁡(β​xk+fk)}\beta_{H,0}=\max\{2.0,\,0.5-\min_{k}(\beta x_{k}+f_{k})\} ensures mj≥0.5m_{j}\geq 0.5. In overdispersed variants, the mean is multiplied by exp⁡(σ​εj−σ2/2)\exp(\sigma\varepsilon_{j}-\sigma^{2}/2) using an independent Matérn field 𝜺\bm{\varepsilon} with range 500​m500\,\mathrm{m} and σ=0.5\sigma=0.5.

On the estimation side, the baseline dictionary 𝒁=[𝑯,𝑭]∈ℝn×199\bm{Z}=[\bm{H},\bm{F}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 199} combines the intercept and linear coordinates in 𝑯∈ℝn×3\bm{H}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 3} with 7×77\times 7 Gaussian kernel grids across four bandwidth scales ℓ∈{600,1000,1800,3200}​m\ell\in\{600,1000,1800,3200\}\,\mathrm{m} in 𝑭∈ℝn×196\bm{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times 196}. Because the knot spacing is approximately 950​m950\,\mathrm{m}, smooth fields 𝒇S\bm{f}_{\mathrm{S}} with medium or long correlation range lie inside or near the column space of 𝒁\bm{Z}, whereas fine-scale variations and the sharp block jumps 𝒖\bm{u} cannot be approximated by smooth kernels and act as residual confounding outside 𝒁\bm{Z}. Varying the parameters in (20) defines four simulation regimes, listed below.

Regime ℓtrue\ell_{\mathrm{true}} (m) a1a_{1} a2a_{2} a3a_{3} ρblock\rho_{\mathrm{block}} Confounding mechanism
A 60006000 0.350.35 0.250.25 0.000.00 0.000.00 Long-range smooth field inside dictionary span
B 12001200 0.350.35 0.250.25 0.000.00 0.000.00 Medium-range smooth field near dictionary span
C 300300 0.350.35 0.400.40 0.350.35 0.650.65 Short-range field plus informative block jumps
D 300300 0.350.35 0.400.40 0.400.40 0.000.00 Short-range field plus uninformative block jumps

Across replications, parameter coverage is the empirical proportion of 90%90\% intervals containing β\beta, and set coverage is the proportion of intervals containing the entire population identification set ΘΓ\Theta_{\Gamma} (Imbens & Manski, 2004). Interval width is the median length over nonempty finite intervals, and the empirical breakdown point is Γ^∗=sup{Γ≥0∣0∉Cn​(Γ)}\hat{\Gamma}^{\ast}=\sup\{\Gamma\geq 0\mid 0\notin C_{n}(\Gamma)\} (Masten & Poirier, 2020).

4.2 Experiment 1. Point Identification under Scale Mismatch

Experiment 1 illustrates Proposition 1 and Lemma  of the Supplementary Material by evaluating competing point-identification estimators across Regimes A–D over 1010 design realizations with R=250R=250 replications each at n=625n=625. Table 1 reports the empirical bias, root mean squared error, and 90%90\% interval coverage for seven specifications, namely (i) unadjusted regression omitting spatial bases; (ii) single-scale penalized Gaussian process regression (ℓ=3200​m\ell=3200\,\mathrm{m}); (iii) the two-stage ‘Spatial+‘ estimator of Dupont et al. (2022), which residuals exposure on a spatial smoother before fitting the outcome model; (iv) precision-weighted restricted spatial regression (‘W-RSR‘) of Khan & Calder (2022), which restricts the spatial random effect to the orthogonal complement of exposure; (v)–(vi) spectral adjustment (‘Spectral‘ h=400​mh=400\,\mathrm{m} and h=1500​mh=1500\,\mathrm{m}) of Guan et al. (2023), which builds on spectral-domain deconfounding (Guillaumin et al., 2022) by damping Fourier modes with wavelengths above h=400​mh=400\,\mathrm{m} or 1500​m1500\,\mathrm{m}; and (vii) the uncalibrated multi-scale orthogonal estimator corresponding to the Γ=0\Gamma=0 limit of our framework. All estimators adjust for the observed covariate 𝑽\bm{V} alongside 𝑯\bm{H}.

Table 1 highlights two main patterns. First, when unmeasured confounding is smooth and long-range (Regime A), methods whose working smoother matches the broad spatial scale (such as single-scale Gaussian process regression, ‘Spatial+‘, fine-cutoff spectral filtering (h=400​mh=400\,\mathrm{m}), and the multi-scale orthogonal estimator) absorb the background trend and maintain coverage near the nominal level. By contrast, unadjusted regression and ‘W-RSR‘ incur substantial bias and severe under-coverage; forcing the spatial random effect to be orthogonal to exposure attributes all shared large-scale variation to exposure while yielding artificially narrow standard errors.

Second, as the true confounding scale shortens (Regime B) and incorporates sharp local block jumps outside the dictionary span (Regimes C and D), single-scale point estimators suffer rapid degradation. While the multi-scale dictionary bridges the scale transition from Regime A to Regime B by combining several kernel bandwidths, even unpenalized multi-scale orthogonalization falls well short of nominal coverage in Regimes C and D. When unmeasured confounding combines unknown fine-scale variations with discontinuous local jumps, no point-identification strategy prevents omitted variable bias, motivating our partial identification approach.

4.3 Experiment 2. Partial Identification under Residual Confounding

Experiment 2 evaluates the joint ellipse projection interval Cn​(Γ)C_{n}(\Gamma) across Regimes A–D over Γ∈{0,0.5,1,1.5,2}\Gamma\in\{0,0.5,1,1.5,2\}. Table 2 reports empirical coverage of β\beta, coverage of the population identification set ΘΓ\Theta_{\Gamma}, the median breakdown point Γ^∗\hat{\Gamma}^{\ast} (Masten & Poirier, 2020), and median interval widths. Because Experiment 1 already establishes that point estimators fail under out-of-span confounding, the bottom panel of Table 2 holds Γ=1\Gamma=1 fixed and compares our joint ellipse projection against competing partial-identification and benchmark sensitivity constructions sharing the same sample summary statistics (β^aug,d^,𝛀^n)(\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}},\hat{d},\hat{\bm{\Omega}}_{n}), namely (i) covariance ablations including an oracle error covariance, an unweighted-residual covariance, a diagonal covariance ignoring Ω^a​d=Cov^​(β^aug,d^)\hat{\Omega}_{ad}=\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}},\hat{d}), and a conservative Bonferroni box; (ii) an unadjusted dictionary benchmark rule that applies omitted-variable sensitivity calibration (Cinelli & Hazlett, 2020; Ciocănea-Teodorescu et al., 2022; Tan, 2024; Dorn et al., 2025) without multi-scale spatial orthogonalization; and (iii) classic one-dimensional partial-identification intervals, the fixed-length endpoint expansion of Imbens & Manski (2004) and the length-pretest refinement of Stoye (2009), applied to the estimated bounds β^aug∓Γ​|d^|\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}}\mp\Gamma|\hat{d}|.

The top panel of Table 2 shows how the partial identification interval restores valid inference under out-of-span confounding. Whereas the point-identified limit (Γ=0\Gamma=0) under-covers severely in Regimes C and D, a modest sensitivity radius (Γ=0.5\Gamma=0.5 or 1.01.0) brings both parameter coverage and identification-set coverage above the 0.900.90 nominal level across all four regimes, including the weak-benchmark setting of Regime D. The empirical breakdown points increase in the out-of-span regimes, reflecting the stronger residual signal captured by the benchmark shift.

In the bottom panel, the feasible covariance estimator based on auxiliary-denoised residuals closely tracks the oracle error covariance in both coverage and interval width, whereas omitting multi-scale spatial orthogonalization (‘Unadjusted dictionary‘) leaves severe smooth confounding bias and under-covers in Regimes C–D. Crucially, the comparison with Imbens & Manski (2004) and Stoye (2009) highlights why standard interval-identification formulas do not carry over to benchmark sensitivity bounds. The half-width Γ​|d0|\Gamma|d_{0}| is a non-differentiable absolute-value functional at d0=0d_{0}=0, so the sample plug-in |d^||\hat{d}| follows a folded-normal distribution and is correlated with β^aug\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}}. Treating β^aug∓Γ​|d^|\hat{\beta}_{\mathrm{aug}}\mp\Gamma|\hat{d}| as smooth Gaussian endpoint estimators causes both the Imbens–Manski and Stoye pretest intervals to fall below nominal identification-set coverage (0.8400.840–0.8860.886) across all regimes and under-cover β\beta under a weak benchmark (Regime D). Projecting the joint two-dimensional ellipse resolves this non-smoothness while yielding substantially tighter intervals than the conservative Bonferroni box.

4.4 Experiment 3. Negative Control Calibration and Diagnostic Checks

Experiment 3 evaluates the three-dimensional negative control calibrated confidence set 𝒞nNC\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\mathrm{NC}} from Proposition 3 and the diagnostic rule 𝒢n\mathcal{G}_{n} in (18) under Regime C at Γ=1\Gamma=1 across R=250R=250 replications. The population mean of the negative control statistic is generated as τNC=ρNC​b0+δshift\tau_{\mathrm{NC}}=\rho_{\mathrm{NC}}b_{0}+\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}, where b0=θa+d0−βb_{0}=\theta_{a}+d_{0}-\beta is the baseline bias of the primary outcome, ρNC\rho_{\mathrm{NC}} is the relative confounding scale on the control outcome, and δshift\delta_{\mathrm{shift}} represents an unmodeled bias discrepancy violating ideal parity.

We examine four configurations of the bridging parameters, namely (i) exact parity (ρNC=1\rho_{\mathrm{NC}}=1, [ρ−,ρ+]=[1,1][\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]=[1,1], ε=0\varepsilon=0, δshift=0\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}=0); (ii) parity within tolerance (ρNC=1\rho_{\mathrm{NC}}=1, [ρ−,ρ+]=[0.8,1.2][\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]=[0.8,1.2], ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05, δshift=0.02\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}=0.02); (iii) moderate scale misspecification (ρNC=1.5\rho_{\mathrm{NC}}=1.5, [ρ−,ρ+]=[0.8,1.2][\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]=[0.8,1.2], ε=0.02\varepsilon=0.02, δshift=0\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}=0); and (iv) severe shift misspecification (ρNC=1\rho_{\mathrm{NC}}=1, [ρ−,ρ+]=[0.8,1.2][\rho_{-},\rho_{+}]=[0.8,1.2], ε=0.02\varepsilon=0.02, δshift=0.35\delta_{\mathrm{shift}}=0.35), creating a major violation of (16). In each scenario, we compare the two-dimensional benchmark interval Cn​(1)C_{n}(1), the three-dimensional calibrated set 𝒞nNC\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\mathrm{NC}}, and a naive difference estimator β^−τ^NC\hat{\beta}-\hat{\tau}_{\mathrm{NC}}.

Table 3 illustrates the dual role of negative control calibration. When the bridging assumptions hold (first two rows), intersecting the negative control constraint with the benchmark ellipse preserves nominal unconditional and conditional coverage while narrowing median interval width relative to Cn​(1)C_{n}(1), with virtually no empty sets. Under moderate scale misspecification (third row), the three-dimensional ellipsoid and posited band [ρ−,ρ+][\rho_{-},\rho_{+}] absorb most of the discrepancy and maintain valid coverage, whereas the naive difference estimator falls noticeably below the nominal level. Under a severe unmodeled shift violation (fourth row), naive differencing suffers a catastrophic loss of coverage; in contrast, our three-dimensional calibration flags the incompatibility between the benchmark and negative control evidence by producing empty confidence sets at an elevated rate, while preserving reasonable conditional coverage among compatible replications in accordance with Proposition 4.

5 Empirical Study

To illustrate the complete partial-identification, negative-control calibration, and diagnostic checking workflow in a large population study, we analyze area-level mortality records across n=6,856n=6{,}856 Middle Layer Super Output Areas in England. The dataset links childhood respiratory mortality records from the UK Health Security Agency Fingertips platform under Indicator 93260 (UK Health Security Agency, 2024) with 1​km1\,\mathrm{km}-grid background nitrogen dioxide (NO2\mathrm{NO}_{2}) concentrations in μ​g​m−3\mu\mathrm{g\,m^{-3}} from the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, 2024), paired with susceptible population denominators 𝒐\bm{o} and population-weighted centroids 𝒔j\bm{s}_{j} from the 2021 Census of the Office for National Statistics (Office for National Statistics, 2021). Separating the effect of traffic pollution from background risk is challenging because neighborhoods near major road corridors experience higher ambient NO2\mathrm{NO}_{2} while also facing socioeconomic deprivation, older housing stock, and uneven access to pediatric care.

To absorb smooth background variation across regional weather patterns, urban–rural gradients, and long-range atmospheric transport, we combine the baseline covariate matrix 𝑯\bm{H} with spatial Gaussian radial basis grids to form a multi-scale dictionary 𝒁=[𝑯,𝑭]\bm{Z}=[\bm{H},\bm{F}]. Because smooth radial kernels cannot capture sharp changes in baseline respiratory vulnerability across neighborhood boundaries and local housing estates, residual confounding 𝒇⟂=(𝑰n−𝑷Z)​𝒇\bm{f}_{\perp}=(\bm{I}_{n}-\bm{P}_{Z})\bm{f} remains outside the column space of 𝒁\bm{Z}. To calibrate this local residual bias and check outcome-side confounding, we pair the spatial dictionary with observed neighborhood morbidity/deprivation benchmarks 𝑽\bm{V} and negative control hospitalization outcomes (unintentional and deliberate childhood injuries under Indicator 93114 and alcohol-related admissions under Indicator 93240; UK Health Security Agency 2024) that satisfy the exclusion condition (15) while responding to the same local socioeconomic gradients.

5.1 Estimation results and partial identification on the England data

We report the four-stage spatial adjustment depth, the partial identification intervals over the sensitivity grid, and the gate diagnostics on the n=6,856n=6{,}856 areas with a complete outcome and exposure record. The offset is person-years in thousands, and the exposure is the standardized annual mean NO2\mathrm{NO}_{2} concentration (mean 11.7911.79, standard deviation 5.335.33), so β^\hat{\beta} is reported per standard deviation of exposure and per 1,0001{,}000 person-years.

Table 4 shows that the coefficient rises from 0.08660.0866 without spatial adjustment to 0.12320.1232 at a single 1010 km scale and to 0.19380.1938 at 4040 km, and returns to 0.12170.1217 with the multi-scale dictionary, which delivers the narrowest of the four intervals. The pattern is non-monotone. The 4040 km basis removes most of the spatially smooth exposure variation and leaves a smaller design, whereas the multi-scale dictionary retains medium-scale variation with essentially the same spatial HAC variance as the 1010 km specification. Every interval excludes zero.

Using the Quality and Outcomes Framework asthma prevalence as the observed benchmark covariate 𝑽\bm{V}, available on n=3,382n=3{,}382 of the areas, we obtain θ^a=0.1695\hat{\theta}_{a}=0.1695 with the benchmark and θ^0=0.1364\hat{\theta}_{0}=0.1364 without it, hence a benchmark shift d^=0.0330\hat{d}=0.0330, a variance ratio rσ=V^a/V^0=0.946r_{\sigma}=\sqrt{\hat{V}_{a}/\hat{V}_{0}}=0.946, a shift ratio κ=|d^|/|θ^a|=0.195\kappa=\lvert\hat{d}\rvert/\lvert\hat{\theta}_{a}\rvert=0.195, and a breakdown point Γ^∗=1.914\hat{\Gamma}^{\ast}=1.914.

At Γ=1\Gamma=1 the interval is [0.0368,0.2937][0.0368,0.2937], and its width grows by 78%78\% between Γ=0\Gamma=0 and Γ=2\Gamma=2. Because the benchmark shift is small relative to the augmented estimate (κ=0.195\kappa=0.195), a modest sensitivity radius stabilizes the conclusion that the exposure effect is positive, and the conclusion becomes inconclusive only once Γ\Gamma exceeds 1.91.9, that is, once unmeasured confounding is allowed to be almost twice as strongly associated with the outcome as the observed benchmark. The positivity of the NO2\mathrm{NO}_{2} effect therefore survives partial identification under a substantial departure from the calibrated benchmark.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

Focusing on additive risk attribution in spatial epidemiology, we have shown how spatial collinearity and latent field flexibility govern the identifiability of environmental exposure coefficients. Combining our operator derivations, simulations, and empirical study yields two main methodological lessons. First, evaluating how a spatial smoother affects exposure estimation requires separating total capacity EDF\mathrm{EDF} from directional overlap ηpen\eta_{\mathrm{pen}}. By Proposition 1, EDF\mathrm{EDF} sums shrinkage factors across all spatial directions, whereas ηpen\eta_{\mathrm{pen}} weights them by exposure energy and directly determines the relative loss of effective Fisher information for β\beta. Reporting EDF\mathrm{EDF} and ηpen\eta_{\mathrm{pen}} together clarifies how much exposure signal a smoother absorbs. Second, estimator performance hinges on how the working basis aligns with the unknown scale of unmeasured confounding (Paciorek, 2010; Bolin & Wallin, 2026; Khan & Berrett, 2026). Overly flexible smoothers absorb local exposure variation and inflate variance, whereas overly constrained smoothers or restricted projections leave unabsorbed regional trends that bias the exposure slope. Rather than relying on fragile point identification under a single smoothing scale, combining a multi-scale dictionary 𝒁\bm{Z} with an observable benchmark variable and a negative control outcome yields valid partial identification intervals Cn​(Γ)C_{n}(\Gamma) and 𝒞nNC\mathcal{C}_{n}^{\mathrm{NC}} across transparent sensitivity bounds, complementing sensitivity analysis under persistent confounding (Tan, 2024; Imbens et al., 2025).

Our local Poisson operator decomposition also extends naturally to mechanistic models and broader spatial settings. Replacing an isotropic kernel with an advection–diffusion Green function rotates the singular vectors 𝒖B,j\bm{u}_{B,j} along physical transport directions, reducing directional overlap ηpen\eta_{\mathrm{pen}} without cutting total capacity EDF\mathrm{EDF} whenever background risk and exposure follow distinct spatial gradients; similarly, replacing β​x​(𝒔)\beta x(\bm{s}) with a bounded dose–response function fmech​(x​(𝒔),ϑ)f_{\mathrm{mech}}(x(\bm{s});\bm{\vartheta}) helps preserve positivity of mjm_{j} while maintaining our two-dimensional diagnostic identities via local gradients. Promising directions for future work include establishing posterior contraction rates under positivity constraints using fixed-domain Gaussian process theory (Li et al., 2024; Ročková & Rousseau, 2024), developing fast approximate inference algorithms (Kündig & Sigrist, 2025; Llamazares-Elias et al., 2026), and extending the diagnostic pair (EDF,ηpen)(\mathrm{EDF},\eta_{\mathrm{pen}}) and joint ellipsoid projection intervals to multi-pollutant mixtures and conditional autoregressive areal models.

Data availability

The England Middle Layer Super Output Area childhood respiratory mortality dataset (Indicator 93260), the Index of Multiple Deprivation and asthma benchmark indicators (Indicator 93275), and the negative control hospital admission series (Indicators 93114 and 93240) analyzed in Section 5 are publicly available from the UK Health Security Agency Fingertips repository (UK Health Security Agency, 2024). Population denominators and population-weighted centroids are available from the 2021 Census of the Office for National Statistics (Office for National Statistics, 2021), and 1​km1\,\mathrm{km}-grid nitrogen dioxide concentrations are available from the UK Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, 2024) under the Open Government Licence.

Supplementary material

Supplementary material available at Biometrika online includes the proofs of Propositions 1–4 and Theorems 1–2, derivations of the working-model bias and variance decompositions, and replication code.
